title: Text Types: VARCHAR vs CHAR vs TEXT
description: Understand character storage in PostgreSQL, debunk the VARCHAR performance myth, and utilize collations.

data.text: In many relational databases (like MySQL or Oracle), `VARCHAR(255)` is faster than `TEXT`. **In PostgreSQL, this is a myth!** Under the hood, `VARCHAR`, `CHAR`, and `TEXT` all use the exact same underlying `varlena` (variable-length array) C data structure.

rows: Recommended default for strings unless length check is a domain constraint
Use when schema must enforce a length limit (e.g. phone numbers, zip codes)
Avoid in modern schemas; whitespace padding wastes storage

data.text: In PostgreSQL all three text types use the same on-disk representation, the `varlena` header. The only difference is that `VARCHAR(n)` and `CHAR(n)` check the length when a value is stored. There is **no performance difference** in reads, indexes, or joins between `TEXT` and `VARCHAR(255)`.

data.title: TEXT, VARCHAR, and CHAR Behave Differently
data.content: Notice the padding and the length semantics.

data.text: `TEXT` ordering and comparison depend on the database collation. With a locale-aware collation, `'a' < 'B'` can be true; with the `C` collation it is false because comparison is byte order. This affects index usability as well as results.

data.title: Sorting, Pattern Matching, and Case Handling
data.code:
SHOW lc_collate;                       -- e.g. en_US.UTF-8

-- Locale-aware comparisons ignore accents/case in some collations. Force a known one:
SELECT 'a' < 'B' COLLATE "C"    AS byte_order,   -- true
       'a' < 'B' COLLATE "en-US-x-icu" AS locale_order;

-- Case-insensitive match: ILIKE, or citext (extension)
SELECT 'Alice' ILIKE 'alice' AS matches;          -- true

-- Index-friendly prefix search needs the pattern operator
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email LIKE 'ada%';      -- can use a btree index with C collation

-- Regex and full-text are different tools
SELECT 'ada@example.com' ~ '^[^@]+@[^@]+$'         AS regex_ok,   -- true
       to_tsvector('english','the quick brown fox') AS fts_vector;

data.text: Use `VARCHAR(n)` only when the limit is a genuine business rule (a two-letter country code, a 20-character licence plate). Preferring `TEXT` plus a `CHECK` constraint conveys the same rule and is easier to change later, because altering a `VARCHAR(n)` length still requires an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock (though it does not rewrite the table).

data.title: Enforcing a Domain Rule With TEXT + CHECK
data.content: Equivalent to VARCHAR(n), but explicit and easy to evolve.

data.title: The `CHAR(n)` Padding Trap
data.text: Values in a `CHAR(n)` column are blank-padded to `n` characters, which surprises anyone comparing them to `TEXT` values and wastes space. There is essentially no reason to choose `CHAR(n)` in a new schema — use `TEXT` or `VARCHAR(n)`.

data.title: Interview Answer
data.text: If asked "is `VARCHAR(255)` faster than `TEXT` in PostgreSQL?", the answer is **no** — they share the same storage format, and only the length check differs. If asked "which should I use?", say `TEXT` with a `CHECK` constraint, using `VARCHAR(n)` only when the limit is a real business rule.

data.title: Prove That Length Does Not Affect Speed
steps: Create two tables with the same 1,000,000 rows: one `t TEXT`, one `v VARCHAR(255)`.
Index each on the column and run `ANALYZE`.
Compare `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE ...` for both.
Show that the plans and buffer counts are equivalent.
data.expectedOutcome: You can cite an experiment, not folklore, in the interview.

items.question: Is there any reason to use `CHAR(n)`?
items.answer: Only for fixed-width values where padding is semantically irrelevant, such as two-character country codes. Even then `VARCHAR(2)` or `TEXT` with a check is clearer.

items.question: How do I store case-insensitive data?
items.answer: Use a unique index on `lower(col)` (no extension needed), or the `citext` extension if you want the column itself to compare case-insensitively.

items.question: What does `n` in `VARCHAR(n)` mean — bytes or characters?
items.answer: Characters. A `VARCHAR(3)` column accepts `'café'` because it is four bytes but three characters.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: There is zero performance penalty for using `TEXT` instead of `VARCHAR` in PostgreSQL.
Use `VARCHAR(n)` strictly to enforce business validation at the database layer.
Never use `CHAR(n)` due to wasteful space padding behavior.
